Name: retrieval_gap_diagnostics
Title: The Knowing-Doing Gap: Diagnosing Why LLMs Store Facts They Fail to Use
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM 'knows' a fact (recoverable via internal probes) but produces a wrong answer, the failure is not primarily a storage problem but a retrieval-routing problem: the fact is encoded in mid-layer representations but never gets copied into the residual stream at the answer position. We hypothesize that this 'retrieval gap' is (1) reliably detectable from internal activations, (2) distinct from cases where knowledge is genuinely absent, and (3) partially fixable via a lightweight, query-agnostic 'retrieval nudge' intervention.
Related Work: Prior work localizes factual recall to MLP lookup mechanisms (Meng et al., ROME/CounterFact; Guo et al. 2024 mechanistic unlearning) and shows LLMs sometimes bypass factual associations via shortcuts (Wang et al. 2024, Knowledge Neurons). Sycophancy work (Wang et al. 2025) shows late-layer override of stored knowledge. Contextually-mediated recall work (Liu et al. 2026) shows recall degrades under indirect queries. Existing work either edits/unlearns knowledge or documents failures behaviorally. Our contribution is different: we build a diagnostic that separates 'knows-but-fails-to-retrieve' from 'does-not-know' cases at the single-example level using internal probes, characterize the layer/position where retrieval breaks, and test a query-agnostic runtime intervention that restores retrieval without editing weights. No prior work provides an example-level knowing-vs-retrieving classifier plus a corrective intervention validated across query paraphrases and multi-hop settings.
Abstract: Large language models frequently produce wrong answers to questions whose answers they demonstrably 'know'—the correct fact is decodable from intermediate representations yet never surfaces in the output. We call this the retrieval gap and propose the first example-level diagnostic to distinguish it from genuine knowledge absence. Using a curated set of factual, relational, and multi-hop queries, we probe whether the correct answer token is linearly decodable at each layer/position via the logit lens and trained probes. We define a fact as 'stored' if it is decodable in mid layers at the subject position, and 'retrieved' if it appears in the residual stream at the final-token answer position. This lets us partition errors into (a) genuine gaps in knowledge and (b) retrieval failures. We characterize where retrieval breaks by tracing information flow from subject to answer positions using attention-knockout and activation patching. Finally, we introduce a query-agnostic 'retrieval nudge': at inference we add the mid-layer subject-position direction that best decodes the fact into the answer-position residual stream, testing whether stored-but-unretrieved facts can be recovered without weight edits. We evaluate on Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama models across query paraphrases, distractor contexts, sycophantic prompts, and 2-hop reasoning. We measure diagnostic accuracy (separating knows-vs-fails), recovery rate of the nudge, and side effects on unrelated knowledge. This provides a mechanistic account of the knowing-doing gap and an actionable, cheap intervention.
Experiments: 1) DATASET: Build a probe set of ~5k queries over CounterFact/relational facts plus a 2-hop subset (e.g., 'the capital of the country where X was born'). For each, verify direct-recall accuracy and construct 5 paraphrases, a distractor-context variant, and a sycophantic-prompt variant. 2) STORAGE PROBE: At the subject token, use logit lens and a trained linear probe per layer to test if the correct answer token is decodable; label each example as STORED or NOT-STORED. 3) RETRIEVAL PROBE: At the final/answer position, decode residual stream at each layer; label RETRIEVED if correct answer is decodable there. Partition errors into knowledge-gap (not stored) vs retrieval-gap (stored but not retrieved). Report the fraction of each and how it shifts across paraphrase/distractor/sycophancy/multi-hop conditions. 4) MECHANISM: For retrieval-gap examples, use attention-knockout and activation patching to identify the layer/head where subject->answer information transfer fails; compare to successful cases. 5) DIAGNOSTIC CLASSIFIER: Train a classifier on internal features to predict, before generation, whether the model will exhibit a retrieval gap; report AUROC on held-out relations. 6) INTERVENTION: Implement the 'retrieval nudge'—extract the best-decoding subject-position direction for the fact and add it (scaled by alpha) to the answer-position residual at the identified layer; measure recovery rate (fixed errors), false-positive rate on genuinely-unknown facts (should NOT hallucinate confidently), and side effects on a control set of unrelated queries (accuracy drop). Compare against baselines: no intervention, CoT prompting, and re-prompting. 7) GENERALIZATION: Test nudge computed on one relation type transferred to another; test across model families and scales. METRICS: partition fractions, probe AUROC, recovery rate, side-effect accuracy delta, calibration on unknown facts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Linear decodability may not equal 'the model knows'—decodable directions could be probe artifacts; we mitigate with causal patching validation and by requiring the direction to causally affect outputs. 2) The nudge may increase confident hallucinations on not-stored facts; we explicitly measure this and treat low false-positive rate as a success criterion. 3) Multi-hop retrieval gaps may be entangled with reasoning failures rather than pure retrieval; we separate these by checking single-hop storage of both intermediate facts. 4) Results may be model/architecture specific (e.g., GQA vs MHA per Venkatesh 2026); we test multiple families to characterize rather than assume universality. 5) Identifying the exact broken layer/head may be noisy; we use aggregate statistics over many examples rather than per-example claims.
